question: Is it wrong to lie?
summary: The Decalogue and a long chorus of prophetic, wisdom, and epistolary texts prohibit lying absolutely — false witness, false reports, deception are abominations. Revelation 21:8 and 21:27 even send liars to the lake of fire. But Exodus 1:18-20 has the Hebrew midwives lying to Pharaoh about why they didn't kill the newborn boys, and God explicitly "deals well" with them for it. Lying merits hellfire in one place and divine reward in another.

reconcile.connective: Defenders split three ways: the reward was mistranslated, it was for the midwives' mercy and not their lie, or there was no real lie at all.

discrepancy.connective: Even within the harmonizing tradition the Geneva annotators concede the deception itself was sinful, which is precisely the point a divine reward strains against.

pd_work.resource: Adam Clarke, Commentary on the Bible (1832), on Exodus 1:19
pd_work.author: Adam Clarke
pd_work.note: Clarke takes up the skeptical charge directly — 'The Hebrew midwives told palpable lies, and God commends them for it; thus we may do evil that good may come of it' — and answers it at length, arguing there was no lie and that God blessed their boldness, not deceit. A passage-specific public-domain defense surfaced on this row.

link.title: Defending Inerrancy: Is there a Bible contradiction in Exodus 1:15–21?
link.note: Live apologetic treatment of God blessing the midwives who deceived Pharaoh, arguing a hierarchy of moral obligations (saving innocent life over obedience to government).

excerpts.excerpt_text: God dealt well with the midwives—This represents God as rewarding them for telling a lie. This difficulty is wholly removed by a more correct translation.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: JFB names the contradiction outright (God appears to reward a lie) and resolves it by re-translation, so 'make a house' = give progeny rather than reward deceit. Directly on the reward-for-lying tension.
excerpts.source_note_text:
God dealt well with the midwives--This represents God as rewarding them for telling a lie. This difficulty is wholly removed by a more correct translation. To "make" or "build up a house" in Hebrew idiom, means to have a numerous progeny. The passage then should be rendered thus: "God protected the midwives, and the people waxed very mighty; and because the midwives feared, the Hebrews grew and prospered."

excerpts.excerpt_text: Their disobedience herein was lawful, but their dissembling evil.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: The Geneva annotators concede within the note that the midwives' deception ('dissembling') was evil, even while approving their disobedience — a verbatim concession that the lie was genuinely sinful, which is the genuine-conflict horn of a reward-for-lying.
